sentences.text: Its skull is described as duck-like, broad, flat, and very elongate, resembling the Late Cretaceous crocodyliform Stomatosuchus.
The animal is known for its exceptionally dorsoventrally flattened, broad, and platyrostral skull, which differs greatly from other caimans.
The osteoderms of the body feature conspicuous spines on their dorsal surface.
Skulls of this genus range up to one meter in length.
A 2020 study estimated the body size of M. amazonensis to be upwards of 9.5 meters and 4.4 metric tons based on skull measurements.
The genus Mourasuchus was first described by Price in 1964.
The initial description was based on a nearly complete skull found in the Solimões Formation of Amazonian Brazil.
The species Mourasuchus arendsi was discovered in the Urumaco Formation of Venezuela in 1984.
By 1990, the genus Carandaisuchus was merged into Mourasuchus, and later studies concluded that M. nativus was a synonym of M. arendsi.
The genus was expanded back to four species with the description of M. pattersoni by Cidade et al.
The short and slender mandibular symphysis suggests the animal likely had a relatively weak bite.
Mourasuchus had slender mandibles and teeth that were not suited for capturing and holding prey like modern crocodilians.
Langston proposed that Mourasuchus may have fed by waiting with open jaws, eating aquatic plants, or sifting through water substrates.
Due to a lack of evidence for filtering, researchers favor the term gulp feeding for Mourasuchus hunting behavior.
It is debated whether Mourasuchus possessed a throat pouch, as no evidence for this structure has been found despite earlier hypotheses.
Mourasuchus was previously classified under the family Nettosuchidae and the genus Carandaisuchus before being synonymized.
Mourasuchus has been firmly placed within the subfamily Caimaninae, though its exact relationships within the family and between species were long unclear.
Recent phylogenetic analyses recover Mourasuchus and Purussaurus as closely related sister genera, with Centenariosuchus just outside this clade.
Mourasuchus lived during the Mid-Late Miocene epoch.
The animal lived between 23.04 and 2.58 million years ago during the Aquitanian to Piacenzian stages.
M. atopus lived in the Peruvian Pebas Formation alongside Purussaurus neivensis, Gryposuchus species, and durophagous caimans.
M. arendsi coexisted in the Urumaco Formation with Purussaurus mirandai, large gharials, durophagous caimans, and Charactosuchus.
Multiple Mourasuchus species are known from the Urumaco and Solimões Formations, including M. pattersoni, M. arendsi, and M. amazonensis.
Mourasuchus lived in Miocene wetlands around 8 million years ago where efficient niche partitioning among diverse crocodilians likely limited competition.
A 2022 study contradicted earlier size estimates, arguing that dorsal cranial length is a poor basis for size estimation compared to skull width.
